stories.title: Nepal flood death toll hits 900 as number missing climbs
stories.summary: The death toll following devastating floods in Nepal has surpassed 900, as rescue teams worked overnight to reach hundreds of people believed to be stuck inside blocked hydropower project tunnels. The country's disaster authority said 903 were now dead, while the number missing in the aftermath also jumped to 4,247. The unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud and debris on the Nepal-Tibet border happened last Wednesday and has been blamed on a glacier collapse. Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, have been buried in shallow graves as they began decomposing in the humid weather in the plains of the Himalayan country after being swept down the mountains by the torrent. Nepali officials said that the focus was on reaching the hundreds of workers believed to be trapped inside about half a dozen hydropower project tunnels that had been blocked by mud and rock debris. Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shovelling mud and rocks under lights in the dark of the night as workers watched.

stories.title: Child remains in hospital after fatal Tyrone attack
stories.summary: A young child remains critically ill in hospital following an attack in a house in Dungannon in Co Tyrone in which a man was killed. A teenage boy arrested on suspicion of murder and attempted murder remains in police custody. Police and paramedics rushed to a house on Lisnahull Road in the town shortly after 11am yesterday after a neighbour reported hearing a woman screaming for help. A man who had sustained serious injuries was declared dead at the scene. A young child was rushed to hospital in Belfast to be treated for serious injuries and remains in a critical condition. A woman treated for non-life threatening injuries has been released from hospital.

stories.title: State lacks dedicated strategy for children in care
stories.summary: As Autumn approaches and the news cycle moves on, questions over the M9 crash will likely fade. Not so for the injured family and their loved ones, the tragedy of that Sunday morning is something they will have to endure for a lifetime. Five families who lost teenagers in the crash, including three members of the Traveller Community, will continue to process their loss. This week, Tánaiste Simon Harris described the issues raised by the crash as "deep-rooted" and "multifaceted", extending across social media, Government, the criminal justice system and road safety. No mention of the care system which formed part of three of the boys' lives; or the juvenile detention centre, Oberstown, which was familiar to one of the teenagers. On the same day he made his remarks, 17-year-old Jack Kennedy’s funeral was under way in Athy. It was the final funeral of the five.

stories.title: Inflation hits estimated 3.4% on new energy price rise
stories.summary: Annual consumer price inflation is estimated to have risen to 3.4% in August from 3.1% July after a monthly jump in energy prices, a flash estimate from the Central Statistics Office shows today. Using the EU's standard for measuring inflation, the CSO said that prices are estimated to have risen by 0.6% between July and August on the renewed energy price pressures, the fastest monthly jump since March. But excluding energy and unprocessed food, price growth slowed year-on-year to 2.6%. Today's CSO figures show that energy prices are estimated to have increased by 4.3% in the month and risen by 11.8% since August last year. Meanwhile, food prices are estimated to have gone down by 0.2% in the last month and gone up by 0.1% in the last 12 months. The corresponding rate for the euro zone will be published tomorrow.

stories.title: Hard-hit areas in Nepal still inaccessible - aid group
stories.summary: Action Aid has said some of the hardest-hit regions in Nepal are still inaccessible following flash flooding and mud slides that have caused devastation along the border with Tibet. Nepal's disaster authority said over 900 were now dead, while the number missing in the aftermath also jumped to 4,247. "One of the hardest hit regions is still not accessible by road," he said. He added he believed that the road was so badly damaged that the conditions don't exist to reach those impacted. "It's raining. Still the monsoon is going on ... they are using the alternative routes. They are facing difficulties and the vehicles are stuck in the mud," Mr Shresta said. Nepali officials said that the focus was on reaching the hundreds of workers believed to be trapped inside about half a dozen hydropower project tunnels that had been blocked by mud and rock debris.

stories.title: The pain & the glory: A look back on Taylor's pro career
stories.summary: Saturday sees Katie Taylor reach the pinnacle. She fights Flora Pili in the main event of a fantastic card of Irish boxing in Croke Park. After much campaigning and conversation, her dream fight is only days away. A fitting swansong after such a successful career. Her professional career began back in November 2016. There has been some of the highest of highs along with some trickier moments. Katie Taylor's professional debut went as well as it could have, considering this was her first experience of the glitz and glamour of the pro game. There was certainly pressure, but she delivered, showing her class and leaving the arena without a scratch. While her opponent was not an unstoppable force, Taylor chalked up her first win. After a quick turnaround, Taylor beat Viviane Obenauf on points to continue her flawless start on the undercard of Anthony Joshua v Eric Molina. Obenauf had to get up off the canvas in round two. This opponent was of better quality as she went on to fight the likes of Chantelle Cameron, Terri Harper and Natasha Jonas. Obenauf is currently serving a prison sentence for the murder of her husband. The third win from three was a dominant victory over Italian Monica Gentili. After winning the opening rounds on the backfoot, the distance closed from the third round onwards with Taylor unloading short punches and uppercuts. Gentili kept marching forward but was dropped early in the fifth round after a flurry of heavy shots. The fight was stopped later in the round.

stories.title: Fourmilewater chasing glory to add to the history book
stories.summary: Championship final day is not a rare thing in Ballymacarbry, it's the norm really. When Comeragh Rangers won the 2024 Waterford Ladies SFC final, it ended the greatest winning run in Gaelic Games history with Ballymacarbry winning 42 titles in a row before that. The Nire too have brought senior football titles back to the village, 11 in all since 1993 with eight final losses bringing the appearance record to over 20 in that spell. But hurling? Hurling has had to play second fiddle to who have given their life to the Nire-Fourmilewater GAA and Ballymacarbry LGFA club on the Waterford-Tipperary border. stories.title: Rangers claim first win of McInnes reign at Aberdeen
stories.summary: Lawrence Shankland's second-half penalty gave Derek McInnes and Rangers some much-needed respite in a 1-0 win over Aberdeen at Pittodrie. The tale of the Light Blues since the Gers boss arrived from Hearts in the summer has been one of constant change in formation and personnel amid exits from two European competitions and a poor start to the William Hill Premiership campaign. The Ibrox side turned in a better performance than many of late and in the 69th minute skipper Shankland, a former Don, converted a spot-kick won by Djeidi Gassama. Aberdeen skipper Kevin Nisbet had the ball in the Gers net in the 81st minute but was judged to have pushed Gers full-back Dujon Sterling and the goal was ruled out. McInnes has brought in 12 new players including debutant Kim Min-su, the 20-year-old South Korean winger signed from Girona on a four-year deal for a reported fee of around £8.5million, and who performed well before he was replaced in the second half. Progress is proving frustratingly slow for the Gers fans but three hard-fought points will bring some positivity to Ibrox.

stories.title: Buttimer strikes again as Munster retain Interpro title
stories.summary: Beth Buttimer haunted Leinster once again as Munster held off their rivals to retain their Vodafone Women's Interprovincial Championship at Dexcom Stadium. Three weeks on from scoring four tries in her side’s 39-19 win against the same opposition, Buttimer scored two more in today’s final in Galway to make it back-to-back Interpro championships for Matt Brown’s side. The hooker’s first score on 20 minutes had given her side a slender 7-5 lead at half time, with Kathy Baker crossing for Leinster shortly before the break. And it would take until the 70-minute mark for either team to add to their total, as Buttimer touched down from the back of a rolling maul, before Enya Breen landed a high-pressure conversion which put her side nine points ahead, and crucially give them a two-score buffer heading into the closing minutes. The afternoon may well have come at some cost for Ireland head coach Scott Bemand, who saw second row Ruth Campbell limp out of the Leinster side in the opening half. Three weeks out from his team’s opening WXV Global Series game against USA in Tallaght, the Ireland head coach will also have some important decisions to make.

stories.title: Star Trek at 60: its secret was exploring humanity, not aliens
stories.summary: When Star Trek first appeared on television screens 60 years ago, audiences expected science fiction to offer aliens, monsters and futuristic technology, writes Stephen McVeigh. From its very first broadcast episode on September 8 1966, Star Trek established that its true subject was the exploration of humanity itself. For all its reputation as an action-packed space adventure, the franchise has endured because it repeatedly returned to a universal question: what does it mean to be human? In that first episode, entitled The Man Trap, the alien antagonist survives by appearing to each observer as the person they most wish to see. Dr Leonard "Bones" McCoy meets a lost love from his past; others see figures shaped by memory, expectation, desire and longing. The creature, soon dubbed the "salt vampire" by fans of the series, is not simply a shape-shifter. Its power lies in exploiting human perception. Rather than asking viewers to fear an alien with superior strength or advanced weaponry, the episode asks a more profound question: can we trust our experience of reality? Watch a clip from The Man Trap, the first Star Trek episode to air in September 1966 Sixty years on, this question looks remarkably prescient. Modern neuroscience increasingly suggests that perception is not a passive recording of the external world. According to theories of predictive processing, the brain continually generates expectations and compares them with incoming sensory information.

stories.title: Katseye's Sophia to miss Dublin world tour opener
stories.summary: Katseye singer Sophia Laforteza will miss the opening night of the group's world tour at Dublin's 3Arena on Tuesday as she continues to focus on her well-being. The 23-year-old will sit out the European and UK leg of the Wildworld Tour, which begins in Dublin on 1 September before travelling to cities across Europe and the UK. The group's management, Hybe and Geffen Records, known as HxG, said: " Sophia is focusing on her well-being, and the company remains fully committed to providing her with all the support and resources needed. "Sophia will not be participating in The Wildworld Tour in Europe and the UK scheduled from September 1 through to September 17. "Our highest priority will always be the health and well-being of our artists." The Dublin opener also comes days after Katseye member Megan Skiendiel sprained her ankle during rehearsals for the tour.

stories.title: McSweeney on how Traitors helped her 'understand people more'
stories.summary:
As she returns to our screens with the second season of The Traitors Ireland, Siobhán McSweeney talks to Claire O'Mahony about her route to an acting career, creating the character of Lady Muck and why she thinks there should be more stories about peasant thighs. For someone uneasy with being treated as a deity, Siobhán McSweeney has an impressive command over the elements. We are midway through a conversation about fame, fandom and treating actors like gods when the lights in the room abruptly go out.

McSweeney, who has just insisted that she is no such thing, takes a moment to reconsider. "Just as I said I wasn’t a god! Nerds! Don’t get any ideas! Oh, maybe I am. I’m a goddess!" As it turns out, they were sensor lights but it was nonetheless a theatrical moment worthy of Lady Muck, the magnificently dressed figure McSweeney created to preside over The Traitors Ireland. She returned to Slane Castle for the second series last weekend, welcoming fresh players into a game of trust, treachery, murder and banishment, with a prize pot of up to €50,000.

The success of the first series answered the question of whether viewers would take to an Irish version of the format, but in the wake of the show’s success came the anxiety of following a hit. "You always have a worry about that difficult second album, don’t you?" says McSweeney, who is originally from the village of Aherla in Cork. "I remember when we did the second series of Derry Girls, there was that, well, we know that people like it…so we knew people liked Traitors, but then the stress was to make sure that you don’t drop the ball or anything. And I can confidently say we haven’t." Best known as the gloriously unimpressed Sister Michael in Derry Girls, for which she won a BAFTA in 2023, McSweeney also presents The Great Pottery Throw Down and has appeared as celebrity chef Della in the hit BBC comedy series, Amandaland.

What has she learned from her first year of Traitors that she’s taken into season two?

"What I learned from last year is that keeping the character of Lady Muck sometimes doesn’t allow the contestants to exhale or relax," she says. stories.title: New personal investment account scheme details revealed
stories.summary: The Government has announced details of a new personal investment account scheme today which, it says, will make investing more accessible to the wider public. The State-backed accounts are expected to be up and running early next year. There will be no minimum contribution, holding or lock-in period for investors. They will also be allowed to move their accounts between providers with no tax liability. The specific tax-free threshold, flat tax rate and annual contribution limit will be announced as part of Budget 2027. Eligible investments will include listed shares, listed bonds, financial instruments traded on a regulated market and a range of investment funds suitable for retail investors, but highly complex and risky products, including derivatives and crypto assets, will not be eligible. The new scheme is part of the Government's Roadmap for the Taxation of Retail Investment plan, which sets out a pathway to simplify and adapt the country's tax framework for retail investment.

stories.title: State-backed investment account offers tax-free threshold
stories.summary: No deemed disposal, a tax-free threshold, and no minimum contribution will be among the key features of the Government's new personal-investment account scheme. It is also understood savers will be able to invest in shares, bonds, and ETFs - however - investing in risky products such as crypto assets and derivatives will not be allowed. Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris is due to announce a roadmap for the new State-backed accounts tomorrow, which are expected to be up and running early next year. Under deemed disposal, every eight years certain investments are treated as if they have been sold for tax purposes - even if there has been no sale. As a result, any gains on such investments are taxed at 38%. The controversial tax is designed to combat tax avoidance. Instead, under the Government's plan, providers will be responsible for calculating, reporting, and paying any tax due to revenue on behalf of investors.

stories.title: Forum recommends tackling energy costs for businesses
stories.summary: Energy has been identified as the principal contributor to rising business costs by an advisory forum established by the Government. The Cost of Business Advisory Forum has issued its final report setting out 63 recommendations to boost competitiveness and cut costs. The report found that the Government should consider the feasibility of a new scheme to reduce prices for large energy intensive business users. It also highlighted the importance of price transparency and easier switching for non-domestic customers. The forum brought together business representative bodies, social partners, regulators, State agencies and Government departments. Members were tasked with examining key non-pay cost drivers affecting enterprise, including energy, insurance, legal services, water and wastewater services, infrastructure and planning, tax administration and regulatory compliance, and banking and financial services.

stories.title: What data tells us about emerging trends in jobs, work and wages
stories.summary: Analysis: Changing work patterns, labour supply and demographics are all shaping the Irish labour market and workplace Steven Lucas is a Senior Statistician in the Central Statistics Office (CSO), and he explains what their data can tell us about employment trends in Ireland. The official estimate of employment is drawn from the Labour Force Survey, where 32,500 households across the country are sampled every three months. Data from this survey allows us to ask different types of households detailed questions on specific elements of the labour market, such as hours worked, type of employment, availability for work, or illness or disability status, which might not be readily available from other data sources. The CSO also harnesses alternative administrative data sources, gathered by other public service bodies and adopted by the CSO for statistical purposes, to provide a timely and accurate picture of the labour market at any given time. Taken together, the CSO's ability to combine administrative and survey data securely and confidentially means we can provide a more complete picture of the labour market in Ireland than any other agency and provide insights on trends over time. Overall, Ireland has seen record levels of employment and low unemployment since the pandemic, but more recent figures show that growth has become more subdued. Our employment rate reached 75.3% in Q3 2024, which was the highest level in the series since 1998. It eased to 74.3% by Q2 2026, although the 2.84 million in employment during that quarter was still the highest level reported in the State. Over that time, the unemployment rate rose to 5.1% from 4.8% in 2025. While the labour market is strong by historical standards, it is important to continually monitor the core indicators for emerging trends.

stories.title: Manhunt under way after woman dies at Swiss rave shooting
stories.summary: A 22-year-old woman has been killed and five people injured, some seriously, in a shooting at a rave party in the Swiss town of Aarau, local police have said. All the victims are Swiss residents and in their 20s, police said, adding a manhunt was under way and large areas of the town had been cordoned off. A witness told Reuters that he heard shots shortly after the music stopped at 2.30am, which he initially mistook for fireworks. Some took cover behind a DJ booth and one woman hid behind a refrigerator, but was fatally shot. "It's just incredibly tragic. She was young," the witness told Reuters. "That something like this could happen in Aarau, at a local event, is simply unimaginable. I still can't really process it." Police said a 22-year-old woman died from her injuries at the scene.

stories.title: Smyth released by New Orleans Saints
stories.summary: NFL franchise New Orleans Saints has released former Down Gaelic footbaler Charlie Smyth following a competitive training camp and a final pre-season game against the Dallas Cowboys, which they won 27-24. They had previously lost pre-season games to the LA Rams and the Jacksonville Jaguars. Smyth had featured in the latter game and missed a field goal. It's something of a surprise given Smyth signed a three-year deal last December. He went into the training camp largely considered the favourite to retain his spot, but the Saints subsequently brought in several other options to challenge the Co Down native. The highest profile of those was former Las Vegas Raiders Pro Bowler Daniel Carlson,  who came in just before the pre-season game and was seen as a major threat to Smyth due to his experience in the league.

stories.title: Tribe veteran on rewarding journey to ultimate glory
stories.summary: A few weeks have now passed since their nail-biting win over Kerry at Croke Park, but Galway's All-Ireland success still feels like a deeply satisfying one for experienced defender Sarah Ní Loingsigh. A senior panellist since 2011, the Naomh Anna Leitir Mór stalwart lined out at full-back when the Tribeswomen collected the Brendan Martin Cup for just the second time in their history with a tense 2-07 to 0-12 showpiece victory at the expense of the Kingdom. The Connacht side had been pushing hard in the latter stages of the championship in recent seasons and their 2026 campaign saw them taking the final step on their journey back to the top of ladies football. This led to scenes of immense joy in the minutes that followed their one-point triumph at the Jones’ Road venue and this mood was maintained upon the squad’s return home to the west a day later. "It was amazing to see family and friends after the game and all the Galway supporters were just so happy and so emotional. It just meant so much to everyone up there and then the homecoming in Tuam the next day was just unbelievable. The scenes and the amount of fans that came out," Ní Loingsigh recalled. "Everyone was just over the moon for the group and the county. It has been a while coming. 22 years since Galway first won an All-Ireland senior title, so it was just such a relief and everyone was so proud of the group. It was lovely seeing how happy everyone was for the team as well."

stories.title: Preview: Hoops seek to park European woes in Derry
stories.summary: Following their disappointment in Finland, Shamrock Rovers will no longer be battling on multiple fronts for the remainder of the 2026 campaign. Stephen Bradley's team have shipped a barrage of criticism in the wake of their exit from European competition, which saw them miss out on the league phase of the Conference League for the first time in three years. There have been gleeful allegations from their domestic rivals that Rovers have "let the league down" and so forth. The rather unfortunate loss to KuPS was pretty forgivable in isolation - the shocking implosion in their second leg against Albanian side Egnatia was much less so. It was especially disappointing given all four of their opponents in Europe this summer came from lower-ranked leagues. After their extra-time defeat to St Pat's in the FAI Cup, it means that the Premier Division programme is all they have left to occupy their time in 2026.

stories.title: Lola Young announces Dublin show after Electric Picnic
stories.summary: Lola Young has announced a Dublin show for next summer, just days after making a surprise appearance at Electric Picnic. Young was a late addition to the Electric Picnic line-up on Saturday, taking to the Main Stage in Stradbally for a surprise afternoon set which included her global hit Messy. The appearance came during Young's return to live performance after she cancelled her 2025 tour and took a break to focus on her mental and physical health following an on-stage collapse in New York. She returned to the stage earlier this year and has since played a sold-out run of UK shows.

stories.summary: Iran has attacked US military targets in the Middle East in retaliation for the first American strikes on its territory in a month, in a fresh flare-up of the war that has engulfed the region. Tehran's Revolutionary Guards said they had retaliated to the attack by striking two US military air bases with ballistic missiles in Jordan, causing "heavy damage". Jordan's army said it had intercepted eight missiles, without stating their origin. The Guards also said they had shot down a US drone over the Strait of Hormuz. The attacks came after the United States said it had attacked Iranian rocket launchers on a small island in the strategic shipping lane. The US said its attacks were aimed at preventing Iran from launching more sea mines into the strait, days after it announced it had completed clearing explosives from the waterway.

stories.title: Door to door sales: How advent calendars became big money
stories.summary:
You might think that late August is far too early to be talking about anything even remotely festive - but Christmas is clearly, already on many people's minds. Or, at least, the days leading up to Christmas. Because, as of now, the wait lists for some of the most sought-after advent calendars are now open. In some cases they’ve been open for weeks. That includes those being sold by some well-known high street retailers, as well as a number of high-end and luxury brands.

But it's not just the high end that is already preparing for December - some retailers are already displaying a wide range of kid-focused advent calendars too. All of these are clamouring to take a piece of what is now a billion-dollar industry, one that's emerged in a little over a decade. The concept of an advent calendar is nothing new, of course. They've been around in some form or another for more than 500 years. For much of that time, they tended to feature Christian-themed imagery as their reward, though eventually many began to offer chocolate too (often tiny, cheap ones).

stories.title: New AI tech considered to tackle wrong-way driving
stories.summary: AI technology and road cameras could be used to alert people more quickly to someone driving the wrong way down a motorway and to help gardaí in their pursuit of the individuals. Minister of State for Road Safety Seán Canney outlined the possible move as he separately said new tougher laws to tackle a spate of recent wrong-way motorway driving incidents will be drafted next week and could be in place by the end of the year. Speaking to reporters at Government Buildings after an initial meeting with gardaí, Transport Infrastructure Ireland and the Road Safety Authority, Minister Canney said it is crucial Ireland makes wrong-way motorway driving an "intolerable" act in this country. The Independent TD said this includes the potential use of AI technology in conjunction with the existing road camera network, which he said could help to better protect the public by providing quicker safety warnings. "There is an opportunity with AI and the camera technology which we have at the moment," he said. He added: "The M50, for example, is well covered with cameras, and on the road to Cork there is a lot of camera networks there.

stories.title: 3 counties now need six figure salary to buy first home
stories.summary: New research shows that a single first-time buyer now needs to earn a six-figure salary to buy a typical first home in three counties. The research from Chill Insurance reveals that a single buyer now needs to earn €108,000 in Dublin, €101,250 in Wicklow and €100,238 in Kildare. Dublin was the only county in that group a year ago. The research also found that in every one of the 26 counties, a single buyer earning the national median salary of €44,816 would fall short of the income required to buy a typical first home because house prices continue to increase faster than wages right across the country. Chill said its research compared the median first-time buyer home price in each county, using the Central Statistics Office's Residential Property Price Index, with median local incomes from CSO earnings data. These figures were then assessed against the standard Central Bank lending rules, under which a buyer can borrow up to 90% of a home's value and up to four times their gross income. Chill said the gap is most severe in Dublin, where the median price for a first-time buyer home now stands at €480,000.

stories.title: Ban on fisted points and handpass limit to be trialled
stories.summary: Gaelic football's Expert Advisory Group are to trial a series of rule tweaks including a ban on fisted points, a limit on consecutive handpasses and a four-point goal in the upcoming third level Division 1 league. The EAG is chaired by former Roscommon and Mayo manager Kevin McStay and was installed on the recommendation of the Football Review Committee in their final report in 2025, charged with monitoring trends within the game following the sweeping rule changes launched in late 2024. The EAG have proposed nine changes which will be trialled in the Ryan Cup this year. A number of more minor tweaks include increasing the number of substitutes from five to six, proposing a 50-metre advancement if a mark is impeded, the extention of the 40m arc to the end-line, and the alignement of all 50-metre advanced frees to the 13m line rather than the 20m line. Speaking today, McStay insisted that their work was concerned with "polishing" and "tweaking" the work undertaken by the Football Review Committee. The other members of the EAG are David Coldrick, John Tobin, Conor McManus, Maurice Fitzgerald, Pat Doherty, Seamus Kenny and Johnny Bradley.
